subtype: Warm welcome to a lonely person [Receiver]
passage: Three weeks after moving to Pune for her master's, and two months after Nani died, Vinita still ate dinner alone in her PG room most nights. So when Pradeep, a smiling boy from her statistics class, said, "We have a small community dinner on Fridays, very chill, come," she almost cried with relief. The flat in Kothrud was warm and smelled of dal. Twelve people knew her name within an hour. A girl hugged her at the door. Someone had saved her a plate. Nobody asked about grades or salaries; they asked how she was, and waited for the answer. There was a short talk about finding your true family, which she half listened to. What she remembered was the feeling, like being wrapped in a blanket. In the auto home she realised she didn't know the group's name, or who ran it. She pushed the thought away. They had already added her to three chats.

qa.q: Where was the Friday dinner held?
qa.a: In a flat in Kothrud.

qa.q: Why did the group feel so good to Vinita?
qa.a: Vinita felt lonely and full of grief, so being welcomed, hugged and asked how she was felt like relief, like being wrapped in a blanket.

qa.q: What could Vinita do before going deeper?
qa.a: She could find out the group's name and who runs it, keep up her other friendships, and notice whether questions are welcome.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see inviting Vinita?
qa.a: Pradeep may genuinely think he is being kind to a lonely classmate, whatever the group's aims, which is part of why the welcome feels sincere.

grounding: Shows a lonely, grieving student invited to a warm group dinner and pulled in by the feeling of being wanted rather than by any ideas.

subtype: Gradual demands on time and loyalty [Receiver]
passage: In January, the Awakening Circle in Hyderabad asked Abhinav for one evening a week. It felt like nothing. In March it was three evenings, plus a "contribution" for the advanced course, where the teacher shared "what the world doesn't want you to know". By May, Abhinav had skipped his cousin's wedding for a retreat and stopped mentioning the group at home, because the seniors said families block your growth. In July he didn't reply to Karthik, his roommate from first year, for eleven days. Karthik had asked one question: "Why do you need permission to visit your parents?" When they finally met at the chai stall near Ameerpet, Karthik laid out the months on a napkin: one evening, three evenings, money, the wedding, secrets. Abhinav stared at it. Each step had felt small, even sensible. Seeing them in a row, his chest tightened. "I didn't decide to do all that," he said quietly. "No," Karthik said. "It got decided a little at a time."

qa.q: How many days did Abhinav not reply to Karthik in July?
qa.a: Eleven days.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel seeing the months written on the napkin?
qa.a: Abhinav felt shaken and uneasy, his chest tightening, as he saw how much had changed when each step had felt small.

qa.q: What made Karthik's approach useful?
qa.a: He laid out the facts in order without insults, letting Abhinav see the whole pattern that is hard to notice from inside.

qa.q: What might Abhinav's family have noticed?
qa.a: They would have seen him miss his cousin's wedding and stop talking about his life, likely leaving them worried and hurt.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose group asked, step by small step, for more time, money, secrecy and distance from doubters, so the total change was hard to see.

passage:
Family counselling note, Thursday.
Usha came in about her son Pankaj, who joined a meditation "family" eight months ago. She described the changes: he no longer argues or questions anything; he calls his old friends "lower-energy people" and has stopped seeing them; most sentences now include the group's words, such as "surrender" and "the Source". He moved into the group's house in March.
In April his father gave him an ultimatum: "Them or us." Pankaj left the dinner table and did not call for six weeks. Usha said, "We pushed him right into their arms."
We talked about staying steady instead: short, warm messages without arguments, his favourite food on Sundays, no insults about the group, and a clear line that home is always open. Usha agreed to try, and to bring her husband next time.
Yesterday Usha sent Pankaj a photo of the mango tree in the yard. He replied with a heart.

qa.q: What did Pankaj's father say in April?
qa.a: He said, “Them or us.”

qa.q: How does Usha feel about the ultimatum now?
qa.a: Usha feels regretful and sad, believing the family pushed Pankaj right into the group's arms.

qa.q: What plan did Usha agree to try?
qa.a: Short, warm messages without arguments, his favourite food on Sundays, no insults about the group, a clear message that home is open, and bringing her husband next time.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have experienced the ultimatum?
qa.a: Pankaj probably felt attacked and forced to choose, which made the group seem like the only place that accepted him, so he stayed away six weeks.

grounding: Shows relatives noticing someone stop questioning, cut ties and speak in a group's language, and learning that warmth keeps the door open where ultimatums did not.

passage:
Last year I was looking for somewhere to belong, and I visited two groups within a month. I'm glad Karthik gave me his four questions first, because on the surface they felt the same: warm, full of purpose, lots of hugs.
Can I ask hard questions? At the gurdwara seva group, when I asked why langar is free for everyone, an uncle laughed and talked with me for an hour, and admitted things he still wondered about. At the Limitless group, when I asked where the fees went, the leader smiled and said doubt was my ego talking.
Can I leave? Some seva volunteers came once a month, some every day; nobody minded. At Limitless, a man who skipped two sessions got calls from five people.
Is the money open? The gurdwara had a notice board. Limitless had "sacred contributions".
Are my outside friends okay? The gurdwara folks told me to bring Karthik. Limitless called him negative.
I, Lokesh, didn't go back to Limitless.

qa.q: What did the Limitless leader say when Lokesh asked where the fees went?
qa.a: The leader smiled and said doubt was Lokesh's ego talking.

qa.q: How did Lokesh seem to feel after that reply?
qa.a: Lokesh seems to have felt uneasy and suspicious, since a fair question about money was brushed off as ego, and never went back.

qa.q: Which test would you advise someone to use with a new group?
qa.a: Karthik's four questions: can I ask hard questions, can I leave freely, is the money open, and are my outside friends welcome.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel being called negative by one group and invited by the other?
qa.a: Karthik might feel stung by the label but reassured by the welcome, and glad the questions helped Lokesh see the difference.

grounding: Shows a person checking whether groups welcome doubt, let members leave, are open about money and accept outside friends, a test a faith community passes and a controlling group fails.

passage: After the video of Yuki tripping in the school corridor went round his class in Osaka, he stopped eating lunch in the cafeteria. At home he stayed up late in a forum where older boys wrote long posts about people like us being laughed at by them, the ones with easy lives. "You're not weak," one wrote to him. "You're awake. You're our brother now." Nobody at school had called Yuki anything but a joke for weeks. The forum had names for everything: the enemy, the plan, the brotherhood. He liked having names. They turned the shame into anger, and anger felt better. One night his older sister Mina, home from university, saw the screen over his shoulder. "Who's them?" she asked. Yuki shrugged. "People who think they're better." Mina didn't argue. She sat on his bed. "Tell me about the video," she said. He was quiet a long time. Then he told her. Later that night she told their mother, and the three of them agreed to see the school counsellor together.

qa.q: What did one forum member call Yuki?
qa.a: Their brother, awake rather than weak.

qa.q: Why did the forum appeal to Yuki?
qa.a: Yuki felt humiliated and alone after the video, and the forum turned that shame into anger and belonging, which felt better.

qa.q: What did Mina do well?
qa.a: She didn't argue about who them was; she sat down, asked about the video to reach the hurt underneath, and brought in their mother and the school counsellor that night.

qa.q: What might Mina have felt seeing the screen?
qa.a: Mina likely felt worried and protective at the talk of an enemy and a brotherhood, but kept calm so Yuki would keep talking.

grounding: Shows a humiliated teenager pulled toward online voices that name an enemy and offer brotherhood, where the draw is belonging more than ideas.

passage: Every night in her room above the family shop in their small hill town, Dolma watched the same channel. A man with a calm voice explained why there were no jobs: the people from the valley town. They took the contracts, they swarmed the market, they were "rats in our grain store". After six months, Dolma watched nothing else. When Nandini, her friend since nursery, said at the bus stand, "Not all of them, Dolma, my Mama married one," Dolma turned away and stopped answering her calls. Then, at the tea shop on Sunday, Dolma heard her own voice say, "Those rats should go back." Across the room sat Mrs Rai, who had taught her maths for free for two years and came from the valley town. Mrs Rai looked down at her cup. Dolma's face burned. Rats. She had said it about a woman who once walked her home in the rain. That night she didn't open the channel. She wrote to Nandini: "Can we talk?"

qa.q: What did Nandini say at the bus stand?
qa.a: “Not all of them, Dolma, my Mama married one.”

qa.q: How did Dolma feel when Mrs Rai looked down at her cup?
qa.a: Dolma felt ashamed, her face burning, on seeing she had called a kind teacher a rat.

qa.q: What warning signs could Dolma have noticed earlier?
qa.a: The dehumanising words like rats and swarmed, watching only one channel, and cutting off Nandini for disagreeing.

qa.q: What might Mrs Rai have felt hearing the words?
qa.a: Mrs Rai likely felt hurt and small, hearing a former student she had helped speak of her people as rats.

grounding: Shows a young adult who comes to see a whole group as less than human, drops a friend who disagrees and watches one channel, until the dehumanising words land on a real person.

subtype: Friend or teacher noticing the shift [Observer]
passage:
Dear Ms Fernandes,
I'm writing about my friend Jatin, second-year mechanical, with his permission.
Over the last four months he has changed a lot. He used to joke with everyone in our hostel wing. Now he talks about "those people" with real contempt, calls whole groups parasites, and watches only one channel late into the night. He has stopped coming to Sunday football and left our old group chat.
At first I argued with him, and he just stopped talking to me. Last week I tried something else. I asked how he was really doing. He told me his father lost his job at the mill in March and the family might lose the house. He said the channel was the only place that explained why. I just listened. I didn't agree, and I didn't fight.
He has agreed to come and see you with me on Thursday at 4. I think he needs someone who can take his anger seriously and help him with it.
Thank you,
Pema

qa.q: What happened to Jatin's father in March?
qa.a: He lost his job at the mill.

qa.q: What seems to lie under Pema's choice to listen instead of argue?
qa.a: Pema felt concerned and hurt when arguing made Jatin stop talking, so chose patience to keep his trust.

qa.q: Why was listening a wiser step than arguing?
qa.a: Listening reached the pain beneath the contempt, the lost job and the house, and kept enough trust for Jatin to agree to see the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel about the channel's explanations?
qa.a: Jatin likely feels scared and angry about his family's troubles, and the channel gives him someone to blame, which feels like an answer.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing contempt for groups, one channel and withdrawal, listening to the pain underneath and bringing in a counsellor.

passage: You want to know how I stopped being angry all the time? I didn't, exactly. I'm Bhavna, and I'm still angry that our basti floods every monsoon while the new towers across the road stay dry. Two years ago that anger went into one page online that blamed a whole community for everything. I shared every post. It felt like a purpose. Then Francis, who runs the youth centre near the station, asked me a strange question: "What would you build, if you could?" Nobody had asked me that. He didn't say I was wrong to be angry. He said, "The flooding is real. Let's measure it." So a dozen of us, Muslim, Hindu, Christian, some who pray and some who don't, mapped every blocked drain with our phones and took it to the ward office. Half the drains were cleared last year. The page still posts. I just don't need it. I'd rather spend Saturdays with people who argue with me and still show up.

qa.q: What did Francis ask Bhavna?
qa.a: “What would you build, if you could?”

qa.q: How did sharing the page's posts make Bhavna feel at the time?
qa.a: Sharing gave Bhavna a feeling of purpose, turning anger about the flooding into blame.

qa.q: How did Francis help without dismissing the anger?
qa.a: He agreed the flooding was real and turned it into a project, mapping drains with a mixed group and taking the map to the ward office.

qa.q: How might people in the mixed group see Bhavna now?
qa.a: They probably see Bhavna as a committed teammate who argues but shows up, not as someone who blames their communities.

grounding: Shows an angry young person who finds varied friends, a real project and an adult who takes the grievance seriously, finding purpose in building rather than hating.

passage: I've told this story to exactly one person, so here goes. Last spring at the agency, Simran, our newest designer, sketched an idea for the bakery chain's campaign on a napkin at lunch: bread rising like a sunrise. It was brilliant. Two days later I presented it to the client as something I had been developing. I didn't mention her. In my head I had reasons. I was the team lead; my name was on the account; credit belongs to the whole team anyway, right? And there was the part I didn't say even to myself: our boss had been praising Simran all month, and I was scared that in a year she'd have my job. The client loved it. I felt sick in the car. When Simran saw the deck, she didn't say anything. She just stopped sharing ideas at lunch. That silence cost the team more than any campaign earned. In June I finally told our boss the idea was Simran's, and I told Simran too. I'm Vandana, and I'm still embarrassed.

qa.q: What was Simran's idea for the campaign?
qa.a: Bread rising like a sunrise.

qa.q: What was Vandana afraid of when taking the credit?
qa.a: Vandana felt scared that Simran, praised by the boss all month, would take Vandana's job within a year.

qa.q: What repair did Vandana make, and what else could help?
qa.a: Vandana told the boss and Simran the truth; naming Simran on the work and inviting her ideas again could rebuild trust.

qa.q: How did Simran respond to seeing the deck?
qa.a: Simran said nothing but stopped sharing ideas at lunch, suggesting she felt hurt and no longer safe offering her work.

grounding: Shows a team lead presenting a junior's idea as their own out of fear of being replaced, telling themselves the team shares credit anyway.

subtype: Seeing your work under another name [Receiver]
passage: You asked why I always put my name and the date on the first slide, Gautam. Let me tell you. I was twenty-four, at a cement company in Nagpur, and I spent three weekends building a model of where our trucks wasted fuel. I emailed it to my manager, Mr Kale, on a Monday. On Friday, at the quarterly review, there it was on the big screen, my charts, my colours, even my spelling mistake in Chandrapur, under his name. The directors applauded him. I sat in the back row, face hot. Angry, yes, but mostly doubting myself. Maybe he had improved it? Maybe asking would make me look petty. So I said nothing. Three months later he did it again with my vendor report. My silence had told him it was fine. The second time, I went to his cabin with my dated emails and said calmly, "I'd like my name on this." He was annoyed. It never happened a third time. Your Raghav sir learned it late. Speak the first time.

qa.q: Which word did Raghav misspell in the charts?
qa.a: Chandrapur.

qa.q: Why did Raghav stay silent the first time?
qa.a: Raghav felt angry but mostly doubtful, and afraid that asking would look petty, so stayed silent.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what did Raghav do?
qa.a: After the vendor report was taken too, Raghav went to Mr Kale's cabin with dated emails and calmly asked for his name on the work.

qa.q: How might Mr Kale have read Raghav's silence after the first time?
qa.a: Mr Kale probably took the silence as consent, which is why he did it again with the vendor report.

grounding: Shows an employee finding their work under a manager's name, feeling anger, doubt and fear of seeming petty, whose silence is taken as consent until they speak.
